clue.text: One with habit assuming this makes bets better?

parts.note: surface reading: a nun somehow improving someone's gambling
setter's reading; if the letter S is replaced by TER, the word bets turns into better

explanation.surface: A nun who wears a habit is credited with making wagers turn out better.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as a statement, S IS TER: assume that and the final S of 'bets' becomes TER, giving 'better'. 'One with habit' is the plain definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A nun is addressed as Sister and wears a habit, the religious robe of her order.

clue.text: "You can't have it away in vehicle" — Tesla's boring motto

indicators.note: something boring drills into the middle of another thing, so these letters sit inside the motto

parts.note: at home means in, as opposed to out
an adage is a saying or maxim
a van is a vehicle
T is the SI symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density

explanation.surface: A slogan for Elon Musk's car company, mocked as dull, about something you can only have in the car.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesla is a unit as well as a car maker, hence T. The definition is a sporting quip: the edge of playing on your own ground is lost when you play away.
explanation.definitionFit: Home advantage is the benefit a team enjoys playing at its own ground, which it cannot have in an away fixture.

clue.text: Drunk on a puree from Provence?

indicators.note: a drunk person is unsteady and jumbled, so the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy eating a purée, perhaps one from the south of France.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as one example among many: Provence is just one part of the continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Provence is a region of France, so anything from there is from a country of the continent of Europe.

clue.text: Behave best housed in squat

indicators.note: something housed in a place is kept inside it, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: to squat is to sit on one's haunches
top means best, as in top marks

explanation.surface: An instruction to be good, set in a squatted building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squat' looks like a noun for an occupied building; here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are commands told to a misbehaving child, telling them to cut it out and be good.

clue.text: Struggling tour is after six elite players

indicators.note: a struggling thing is twisting and contorted, so the letters that follow are reshuffled
after places the reshuffled words behind the number that follows, reversing the clue's order

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
the six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A band of half a dozen top players finding a tour heavy going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the anagram behind the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Virtuosi are performers of outstanding technical skill, the elite of musicians.

clue.text: Branch in Oregon stocks fabric

indicators.note: a shop that stocks goods keeps them inside, so the answer is held within the words

parts.note: found running across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A shop's Oregon branch keeps a particular cloth in stock.
explanation.definitionFit: Chino is a hard-wearing cotton twill cloth, the material of chinos trousers.

clue.text: Silly cleaner's last in line for promotion

definitions.note: a noun here: a silly is a foolish person

indicators.note: one thing in for another stands in its place, so a letter swaps with a word inside

parts.note: a charlady is a woman paid to clean a house or office

indicators.note: the last in a sequence is its final member, so only the end letter is used

parts.note: final letter of the word
an ad promotes a product

explanation.surface: A cleaner seems to be next in the queue for promotion at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last in line for promotion' reads as one phrase about a job queue, but it splits into a single letter and the word it replaces. A charlady is an old British word for a woman cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a charley is a fool, as in 'a right charley', so it works as a noun for a silly person.

clue.text: Fanatic uttered greeting imitating Sopranos?

parts.note: an ultra is an extremist or fanatical supporter

indicators.note: uttered means spoken, so the word is wanted for how it sounds rather than its spelling

parts.note: hi is a greeting, and high is said the same

explanation.surface: A fan says hello while doing an impression of Tony Soprano and his TV mob family.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sopranos looks like the TV crime drama; here sopranos are singers with the highest voices, and the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sopranos sing at the top of the vocal range, so mimicking them means producing extremely high-pitched notes.

clue.text: See 2
Snatch pig from shallow passageway

indicators.note: to snatch something is to grab it away, so these letters are taken out of the longer word

parts.note: taken as written
a sow is a female pig

explanation.surface: An instruction to grab a pig out of a shallow trough or pool.
explanation.walkthrough: The three letters S, O and W are not together in the word: they are lifted from the start and the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A hall is a corridor or entrance passage in a house, a synonym for passageway.

clue.text: Extravagant red coat in 20s style

indicators.note: extravagant suggests something wild and unrestrained, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A flamboyant scarlet coat cut in the fashion of the Roaring Twenties.
explanation.definitionFit: Art deco was the bold geometric design movement that flourished in the 1920s and 1930s.

clue.text: Partner takes divot striking 3-wood at last — that's decisive

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so the partner word wraps around the other

parts.note: a pal is a friend or partner

indicators.note: striking something out removes it, so a letter is struck from the word
at last points to the final letter of the club name, which is the one struck out

parts.note: taken as written: a clod of turf cut out by a golf shot
the club's final letter

explanation.surface: A golfing partner's divot, dug while hitting a fairway wood, proves the turning point of the round.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf scene hides the mechanics: a 3-wood is a golf club, but here only its last letter matters, and that letter is knocked off the front of divot.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pivotal is of central, deciding importance, like the pivot on which everything turns.

clue.text: Beginners in lush uncut rough can't handle pitch

indicators.note: beginners are the starting points, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Novice golfers in thick unmown rough can't cope with the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' looks like the golf shot or the playing area; it is the verb for a sudden tilt, as a ship does.
explanation.definitionFit: To lurch is to make a sudden unsteady roll, the same movement as a ship pitching in heavy seas.

clue.text: Terrible tsunami disheartened Haitians — they can't imagine life after this

definitions.text: they can't imagine life after this

indicators.note: something terrible is a wreck, so the letters are knocked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: without its heart a word loses its middle, so only the outside letters are left

parts.note: first and last letters only

explanation.surface: A catastrophic tidal wave leaves the people of Haiti despairing of the future.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They can't imagine life after this' sounds like grief for the disaster's victims; 'this' is life itself, and the definition describes people who reject an afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: Humanists hold a non-religious outlook and do not believe in any existence after death.

clue.text: Old men, clothing XS, showing muscle

indicators.note: clothing goes around a body, so one pair of words wraps around the other

parts.note: ex- means former
OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
X is ten in Roman numerals, so XS reads as tens

explanation.surface: Retired soldiers squeezed into extra-small clothes, showing off their physique.
explanation.walkthrough: XS looks like the clothing size extra small, but it is a plural: several Xs, that is tens.
explanation.definitionFit: An extensor is a muscle whose contraction straightens or extends a limb, the opposite of a flexor.

clue.text: Yeovil's original tough guy denied opening as farm worker

indicators.note: denied its opening means refused its start, so the first letter is dropped
the original part of something is where it starts, so only the town's first letter is used

parts.note: first letter of the Somerset town
a hard man is a tough, aggressive man

explanation.surface: A hard man from Yeovil, a Somerset town, is turned away and ends up working on a farm.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardman is a labourer who works in a farmyard or other yard, doing general jobs.

clue.text: Defeat 3-1 results in long ball strategy

parts.note: a rout is a crushing defeat
the answer to 3 down is EUROPEAN, abbreviated E
the numeral spelt out

explanation.surface: A football scoreline: losing three-one comes from just hoofing the ball forward.
explanation.walkthrough: The score 3-1 is two separate pieces: 3 points to the answer of 3 down, European, whose abbreviation is E, and 1 is ONE. Route one is British football jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: In football, route one is the direct tactic of hitting long passes straight up to the forwards, skipping midfield build-up.

clue.text: Exhibiting is arduous

explanation.surface: Putting on a show is hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear an expression is to show it, and a wearing task is one that wears you down, so is exhausting.

clue.text: Lost fortune and, given time, travelled by public transport

parts.note: went means travelled
a bus is public transport
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone who lost all their money and, in time, had to take the bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given time' tacks the letter on after the transport.
explanation.definitionFit: To go bust is to become bankrupt, having lost everything one had.

clue.text: In a state, blokes scratching backsides

indicators.note: scratching out the back ends means removing each word's final letter

parts.note: two men's names, George and Ian, standing for blokes

explanation.surface: Men so agitated they are scratching their behinds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a state' reads as worked up; the definition is just 'a state', a US one. Blokes can be any male names; here George and Ian each lose their last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgia is one of the fifty United States, in the south-east, with Atlanta as its capital.

clue.text: Excited to find new course west of Estepona: cue round!

parts.note: a turn is a change of direction

indicators.note: the westernmost part of a word on a map is its left end, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of the Spanish resort town

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a nod is a signal or cue to act

explanation.surface: Thrilled to discover a new golf course near Estepona, a Spanish resort: time for a round!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a round of golf, but it reverses the cue.
explanation.definitionFit: Turned on means aroused or excited, informally.

clue.text: See 28
Partially reupholster a Torino, an old relative of Clio

indicators.note: partially means only in part, so the answer is a piece of the words that follow

parts.note: found across the end of the first word, the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A car restorer re-covers a Torino's seats, an old Ford model, like a Renault Clio's ancestor.
explanation.walkthrough: Torino and Clio look like car models; Clio is the Muse of history, and the answer is another of the nine Muses, her sister.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Muse of lyric and love poetry, a sister of Clio among the nine Muses of Greek myth.

clue.text: Cycling fast, more accomplished than the rest

indicators.note: cycling means going round in a loop, so letters from the front are moved around to the back

parts.note: fast means firmly fixed, as in stuck fast

explanation.surface: A quick cyclist outperforming the rest of the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speed; it means firm or secure.
explanation.definitionFit: Ablest is the superlative of able, so it means the most capable of all, better than every other.

clue.text: Tip for horseradish: removing skin fully, peel

indicators.note: the tip of something is its point or end, so just the first letter is wanted

parts.note: first letter

indicators.note: taking the skin off leaves only the inside, so the outer letters are lost

parts.note: inner letters, without the first and last

explanation.surface: A kitchen tip on preparing horseradish root: strip it completely.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as cookery advice; 'peel' is the verb, and to hull is to strip husks.
explanation.definitionFit: To hull is to remove the outer covering or husk of a fruit or seed, a synonym of peel as a verb.

clue.text: Implement bizarre resolution to liberate Roo

indicators.note: bizarre means weird and out of order, so the remaining letters are rearranged
liberating something lets it go free, so those letters leave the word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Put into effect a strange decision to free Roo, the young kangaroo from Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Implement' looks like a verb at the start; it is the noun, a tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A utensil is a tool or implement, especially one used in the kitchen.

clue.text: Champion's loss initially placed on 'self-inflicted wound' pile

parts.note: to champion a cause is to back it

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the word's first letter is taken

parts.note: first letter
OG is an own goal, a football mistake that wounds your own side

explanation.surface: A champion's defeat is put down to a self-inflicted error, adding to a pile of woes.
explanation.walkthrough: An own goal, OG, is when a player puts the ball in their own net, hence a self-inflicted wound.
explanation.definitionFit: A backlog is an accumulated pile of work or matters still waiting to be dealt with.

clue.text: Mizuno's latest clubs held in firm palm

indicators.note: something held in another is enclosed by it, so these letters go inside

parts.note: Co is short for company, a firm

indicators.note: the latest is the most recent, the one at the end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of the sports brand's name
C is the card suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: Golf clubs from Mizuno, the Japanese maker, gripped in a steady hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palm' looks like the hand; it is the tree. Clubs and firm both suggest golf grips but give card and business letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Coco is the coconut palm, the tropical tree that bears coconuts.

clue.text: Driving can produce these unexpected outcomes

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in golf, hitting a ball off the tee with a driver sends it a great distance
second meaning: results thought very unlikely, at long odds

explanation.walkthrough: Driving suggests a car but means a golf drive; the second meaning comes from betting odds.
explanation.definitionFit: Drives off the tee travel far, and outsiders with little chance of winning are called long shots too.

clue.text: A popular destination, Southern Dales left Coot refreshed

indicators.note: something refreshed has been made over anew, so the gathered letters are put into a new order

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left
the setter's own name, taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter leaves the Yorkshire Dales in the north for the south, and returns revived from a favourite holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Coot is the setter of this puzzle, so the setter's name is fodder here. The Dales are hill country in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Costa del Sol on Spain's southern coast is one of Europe's best-known package-holiday regions.
